cues.say: Meet P G Lion, a new kind of index for Postgres.
cues.cap: Meet pg_lion, a new kind of index for Postgres.

cues.say: It's built to answer one question very fast: how many rows match?
In the next few minutes: how it works, how it compares with the B tree and gin indexes you already use, and when to reach for it, and when not to.
Dashboards, search filters and reports keep asking the same kind of question.
How many events came from Japan? How many of those were purchases? How many per country?
In SQL, that's count star, with a WHERE clause, and often a GROUP BY.
cues.cap: In SQL, that's count(*), with a WHERE clause, and often a GROUP BY.

cues.say: Our example table has five million rows, and half of them match.
So Postgres has to count two and a half million rows. How long that takes depends on the index.
Start with the B tree, the index Postgres gives you by default.
A B tree is a sorted list of keys, like a phone book. Each entry points to one row in the table.
Finding a key is quick: a few hops down the tree, and you're there.
That's why B trees are so good at fetching a few rows, reading ranges in order, ORDER BY with LIMIT, and enforcing uniqueness.
But to count, a B tree walks its entries one by one, and hands every single row to count star.
cues.cap: But to count, a B-tree walks its entries one by one, and hands every single row to count(*).

cues.say: Two and a half million matches means two and a half million steps. On our test machine, that took about a hundred and fifty-seven milliseconds.
cues.cap: 2.5 million matches means 2.5 million steps. On our test machine, that took about 157 milliseconds.

cues.say: Gin turns that around. It's an inverted index.
For every key, a word, a tag, or a JSON value, it keeps a list of the rows that contain it.
cues.cap: For every key (a word, a tag, or a JSON value) it keeps a list of the rows that contain it.

cues.say: That's exactly what arrays, JSON-B and full-text search need, because one row can hold many keys.
cues.cap: That's exactly what arrays, JSONB and full-text search need, because one row can hold many keys.

cues.say: Its keys are sorted, so gin can match a prefix, and it narrows phrase searches before checking the table.
But for a count, gin can only hand Postgres a bitmap of matching rows. Postgres then reads the table pages and counts rows there.
Our count took about six hundred sixty-five milliseconds.

scenes.title: Lion: sets of rows, in chunks

cues.say: Lion is an inverted index too: every key maps to the set of rows that have it, just like gin.
What's different is how that set is stored.
Lion splits the table into chunks of sixty-four pages. For each key, each chunk gets one small container.
cues.cap: Lion splits the table into chunks of 64 pages. For each key, each chunk gets one small container.

cues.say: Each container takes whichever shape is smallest.
Only a few matching rows? A short sorted list.
Lots of them? A bitmap, with one bit for every row slot in the chunk.
Long unbroken stretches? Just a start and a length.
This trick is called a roaring bitmap. Hence, the lion.
And every container records how many rows it holds.
So Lion doesn't walk rows to count. It adds up the containers' totals: one step per chunk, instead of one step per row.
There's one catch, and it's the same one index-only scans have.
An index can't tell whether a row is visible to your transaction. Only the table knows.
So Postgres keeps a visibility map: one flag per table page, meaning every row here is visible to everyone. Vacuum sets those flags.
cues.cap: So Postgres keeps a visibility map: one flag per table page, meaning every row here is visible to everyone. VACUUM sets those flags.

cues.say: Where the flags are set, Lion trusts the container's total.
Where a page changed recently, Lion checks those rows in the table, one by one. So the answer is always exact.
The result: the same count in one point seven milliseconds. Ninety times faster than the B tree, and nearly four hundred times faster than gin.
cues.cap: The result: the same count in 1.7 milliseconds. 90× faster than the B-tree, and nearly 400× faster than GIN.

cues.say: Because every set is a bitmap, combining filters is cheap.
Country is Japan, and type is purchase? Lion lines up the two sets chunk by chunk, keeps the overlap, and counts it.
GROUP BY works the same way: one count per key, without reading the rows.
In our benchmark, two filters ran about nine times faster than the B tree, and counting two hundred groups about twenty-four times faster.
cues.cap: In our benchmark, two filters ran about 9× faster than the B-tree, and counting 200 groups about 24× faster.

cues.say: A thousand-value IN list, or a range, about two and a half times. And counting array tags beat gin by up to a hundred and sixty-eight times.
cues.cap: A 1,000-value IN list, or a range, about 2.5×. And counting array tags beat GIN by up to 168×.

cues.say: Now, the honest part. Lion isn't a better B tree, and it isn't a better gin.
Looking up a rare key is a tie: both finish in tens of microseconds.
Fetching the matching rows is a tie too, because reading the table dominates.
Lion can't return rows in order, so ORDER BY with LIMIT needs a B tree. So do unique constraints and primary keys.
Lion stores no word positions, so phrase and prefix searches belong to gin.
Frequent changes slow it down. After updating one percent of rows without a vacuum, our count went from under two milliseconds to eighty-one. Still well ahead of the B tree, but the gap shrinks.
cues.cap: Frequent changes slow it down. After updating 1% of rows without a VACUUM, our count went from under 2 ms to 81 ms. Still well ahead of the B-tree, but the gap shrinks.

cues.say: And writes cost more. Inserts were about a quarter slower than with B trees, wrote about one and a half times the write-ahead log, and index builds took nearly three times as long.
cues.cap: And writes cost more. Inserts were about 25% slower than with B-trees, wrote about 1.5× the WAL, and index builds took nearly 3× as long.

cues.say: Using Lion is plain SQL.
Create the extension, add Lion indexes on the columns you filter and group by, then vacuum analyze the table.
cues.cap: Create the extension, add Lion indexes on the columns you filter and group by, then VACUUM ANALYZE the table.

cues.say: Write your queries as usual. There are no special functions to call.
In EXPLAIN, look for Custom Scan, Lion Count. That means the count came straight from the index.
cues.cap: In EXPLAIN, look for Custom Scan (LionCount). That means the count came straight from the index.

cues.say: For range queries on timestamps or ID columns, build the index with summaries set to auto.
cues.cap: For range queries on timestamps or ID columns, build the index WITH (summaries = auto).

cues.say: And keep your other indexes. Lion, B tree and gin can all sit on the same table.
So, the short version.
Counting, filtering and grouping, for dashboards and facets: Lion.
Fetching rows by key, ordered results, and uniqueness: B tree.
Full-text phrase and prefix search, and JSON documents: gin.
Busy, write-heavy tables that rarely get vacuumed: measure carefully first.
P G Lion is still a prototype. These numbers come from one benchmark, on PostgreSQL eighteen with five million rows. Measure it on your own data before you depend on it.
cues.cap: pg_lion is still a prototype. These numbers come from one benchmark, on PostgreSQL 18 with 5 million rows. Measure it on your own data before you depend on it.
